query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.

System: WVTaTiCr x (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings on 42-CrMo steel substrate. Processing: Laser cladding using a LYHS series ultra-high-speed laser-cladding machine; powder mixture of W, V, Ta, Ti, Cr (45–105 μm, 99.9% purity) ball-milled for 24 h at 300 r/min (10:1 ball-to-material ratio); laser power 1.4 kW, scanning speed 8 mm/s, spot diameter 6 mm, overlap rate 30–40%, argon protective gas. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
